description:
A Roman settlement in Hambleden, situated alongside the Hamble Brook, was identified in the 1990s through cropmarks. The Historic Environment Record (HER) suggests this may be the site of a temple due to the presence of a rare hexagonal structure, measuring 12 meters across, featuring a central pit. This structure is visible in aerial photography within a large square enclosure.

Polygonal temples are a recognised architectural tradition in Roman Britain and provide strong parallels to this site; notable examples include the temples at Pagans Hill and Weycock Hill. Because polygonal forms are rare in domestic or agricultural contexts, and central pits often indicate depositional activity, these features strongly support its identification as a religious building. As no excavations have yet been conducted, there is no precise dating available beyond its classification as a Roman-era structure. While polygonal temples are most commonly associated with the 2nd century AD onwards, an earlier date remains possible.
